title: Authorization Models: RBAC, ABAC, and Relationship-Based Access (Zanzibar)
lesson:
Authentication answers who you are; authorization answers what you may do. Role-based access control (RBAC) assigns permissions to roles and roles to users, so an 'editor' role can edit documents. It is simple to audit and works well when job functions are coarse, but it suffers role explosion once you need distinctions like 'editor of only the marketing team's documents in the EU'.

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) evaluates a policy over attributes of the user, the resource, the action, and the environment, for example 'allow if user.department == resource.department and time is within business hours'. It is far more expressive and needs no per-resource grants, but policies are harder to reason about and test, and reverse questions like 'who can see this file?' are hard to answer.

Relationship-based access control (ReBAC), popularized by Google's Zanzibar paper, stores access as a graph of relationship tuples such as 'user:alice is editor of doc:42' and 'folder:7 is parent of doc:42', then derives permissions by traversing the graph, so access to a folder can inherit to its documents. This fits products with sharing, nesting, and organizations, and supports both 'can Alice view this?' checks and 'list everything Alice can view' queries. The cost is a dedicated, highly available authorization service and care around consistency: Zanzibar uses tokens (zookies) so a check never evaluates against data older than a recent permission change.

Whatever the model, enforce authorization on the server at every access, deny by default, centralize the decision logic rather than scattering ad hoc checks, and log decisions. Cache decisions only with short lifetimes, because a revoked permission that lingers in a cache is a security bug.

questions.prompt: A product lets users share documents with individuals, groups, and nested folders, and needs 'list everything Alice can view'. Which model fits best?
options: Flat RBAC with one role per document
Network ACLs on the load balancer
questions.explanation: A relationship graph supports inheritance through folders and can answer both check and reverse-lookup queries.

questions.prompt: Role explosion is a common scaling problem of RBAC when permissions depend on many resource-specific distinctions.
questions.explanation: Each distinct combination of scope and permission tends to need its own role, so role counts grow quickly.

questions.prompt: Authorization systems should follow a ____-by-default policy: access is refused unless a rule explicitly allows it.
questions.explanation: Default deny ensures that gaps or missing rules fail closed rather than open.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Zanzibar's consistency tokens (zookies)?
options: To ensure a check is not evaluated against data older than a recent permission change
questions.explanation: Zookies let a client say 'evaluate at least as fresh as this write', avoiding stale-permission anomalies.

questions.prompt: Order the evaluation of a ReBAC check, earliest first.
items: Traverse relationship edges from the user toward the resource
Receive the check: can user U perform action A on resource R
Combine results of the permission's rewrite rules
questions.explanation: A check starts as a request, walks the tuple graph, combines inheritance rules, then returns a decision.
